objective.title: Approach optimal play through robust self-play
objective.summary: The long-term goal is approximate optimal / equilibrium-oriented play in the closed-team-sheet VGC game. Measure progress across held-out teams and a varied opponent set; report average, lower-percentile, and worst-case results. No single opponent or fixed win-rate threshold defines completion.

candidate.label: Current in-battle policy vs Round424 start
candidate.status: Current validated candidate · Round436 ablation and external screens inconclusive
candidate.note: Round431 scored 49.36% [45.85%, 52.93%] against Round430, and Round432 scored 47.90% [44.29%, 51.61%]; neither showed a clear gain. Round430 remains the validated in-battle candidate. Round402's 77.15% result is a separate team-preview selector benchmark. Round432 external screens also showed no clear lift: all paired 95% intervals vs Round430 and Round431 include zero. Round432 cross-opponent equal-weight mean/median/p10/worst were 60.35%/48.83%/47.64%/47.46%; the mean is buoyed by random play. Round435 used a Round434 restricted-game mixture (31.7% Round430 / 68.3% Round432 in the policy pool) and scored 52.98% [49.41%, 56.59%] head-to-head with Round430; all matched external deltas vs Round430/432 included zero. Round430 remains the candidate. Round436 removed hidden-set auxiliary loss on the identical Round435 data; it scored 53.42% [49.80%, 56.93%] vs Round435 over 512 clusters (one incomplete game), an inconclusive ablation. Round430 remains the validated candidate. Round436 external screens at 256 clusters found no supported paired gain vs Round435: deltas on 128 shared clusters were +0.20 pp vs Max Damage [-0.59,+0.98], +0.39 pp vs public Counterplay [-0.59,+1.37], 0.00 pp vs random [-0.78,+0.78], and -0.20 pp vs Round102 [-0.98,+0.39]. Round436 remains unpromoted; Round430 is still the validated candidate.

speed.context: Round430 20,000-game complete training iteration including rollout and PPO preparation/optimization; Round435 full aggregate rollout telemetry was not captured. Not raw simulator speed.
speed.decision_latency: ~85 ms action selection per policy-pool match
speed.current_bottleneck: Rollouts: policy inference/action selection, observation encoding, and public-counterplay scoring. PPO update: audited record-to-transition preparation, 169.1 s for 20k games (Round447); Round453 trimmed full model-input construction 7.1%, estimating 1.28 s saved per update, not yet replay-validated.
speed.gpu_status: RTX 4060 used for PPO optimization; rollout inference and Showdown simulation remain CPU-side
speed.profile_context: Round430 remains the latest complete end-to-end 20,000-game profile: eight-worker rollout 22.55 games/s and full iteration 16.49 games/s. Round435 offers newer per-shard timings but no valid aggregate rate after preflight recovery. Per-opponent shard rates are not aggregate rates. Action selection contains policy inference; Public Counterplay scoring is nested inside action selection.

active_training_profile.status: Round435 per-worker profile · Round430 retained as candidate
active_training_profile.context: Round435 single-shard timing samples from 20,000-game PPO update, after seat-balanced recovery from one duplicate-team record. The wrapper did not capture full-run aggregate rollout telemetry. Do not sum per-shard rates as aggregate.
active_training_profile.finding: Round435 measured about 76 ms/match of Public Counterplay scoring, 65–73 ms/match policy inference against pool opponents, and 28–37 ms/match Showdown engine time. PPO record preparation plus tensor aggregation took 159.3 s for 20,000 games, versus about 55 s optimization. Improve automatic duplicate-team recovery, then prioritize batched policy inference and audited record parsing/tensor preparation. A CPU microbenchmark of PPO model-input construction found 16.4% lower stage time by reusing cached static tensors rather than cloning them per state; linear extrapolation is 3.76 s over 162,366 transitions, still awaiting full-iteration confirmation. A targeted public-mechanics scalar-clip change cut transition extraction by 22.5% on 1,971 real states, with exact feature parity; estimated saving is 6.66 s per 162,366 transitions, pending end-to-end validation. A fresh Round441 full PPO replay took 226.3 s for sample collection and about 290 s wall time. All 82 final checkpoint tensors matched Round437 exactly, but the run was slower than both prior replays, so isolated preprocessing gains are not yet proven end to end. A subsequent observation-array reuse microbenchmark cut transition extraction by 7.1% with exact transition parity, estimating 1.62 s saved over 162,366 transitions. It postdates Round441 and still needs full-run validation. Precomputing static hidden-set targets per record yielded 4.2% lower extraction time with exact parity, estimating 0.90 s saved per Round435 rollout; post-Round441 and not yet tested end to end. Round447 then used a strict-audit byte-offset index and full row validation: 169.12 s sample preparation for 20,000 games (25.3% below Round441), with exact metrics and checkpoint parity to Round437. Full replay was ~232 s, still ~14 s slower than Round437; this does not establish a faster end-to-end iteration.

opportunities.title: 1 · Keep per-worker CPU inference at current concurrency
opportunities.detail: Round449 tested a shared CUDA inference queue against independent CPU model processes at 8 and 16 producers. With a 1 ms batch window, CPU reached 2,850 / 3,530 states/s and GPU reached 1,606 / 2,912; CPU also had lower p95 latency. A 3 ms GPU wait made throughput worse. Do not add a GPU broker at these worker counts. Reconsider only if real rollouts can sustain larger batches and the memory budget supports more concurrent matches; the prototype excludes IPC and live feature preparation.

opportunities.title: 2 · Cache static team tokens and trim observation encoding
opportunities.detail: Round448 added a per-match PolicyAgent cache for static species/move/item/ability tensors. On 1,971 real states, live model-input construction fell 26.8% (0.4680 s to 0.3424 s) with exact input parity; a deterministic policy action, log probability, and value also matched. Linear extrapolation is 10.34 s per 162,366 PPO states, not whole-match evidence. Next measure games/s and p95 decision time, then profile remaining dynamic observation and public-mechanics encoding.

opportunities.title: 3 · Batch rollouts and tune worker count
opportunities.detail: A fixed 240-game Max Damage benchmark measured 30.94 games/s at 8 workers, versus 29.09 at 12 and 26.04 at 16; memory also rose from 6.77 GB at 8 to 13.25 GB at 16. Keep 8 as the measured setting for now. Test batching requests across those workers before increasing concurrency.

opportunities.title: 4 · Reduce counterplay scorer cost
opportunities.detail: A per-decision cache for repeated public damage calculations cut scorer time from 203.4 to 62.6 ms/match (69%) in a paired 32-game single-worker probe. In a separate 240-game, 8-worker run, scoring averaged 80.1 ms/match and aggregate rollout throughput was 23.51 games/s, with no timeouts or corrections. Still compare an 8-worker pre-cache control and rerun the full mixed PPO iteration; then profile repeated speed and legality calculations.

opportunities.title: 5 · Index audited PPO records for training
opportunities.detail: A fresh strict audit of the 3.87 GiB Round435 set writes byte offsets for its 20,000 valid trainable views. The trainer seeks to those rows and still validates each one, avoiding parsing and transition preparation for the opponent views and invalid records. Round447 prepared 162,366 transitions in 169.12 s, 25.3% below Round441; all 82 checkpoint tensors matched Round437 exactly. Full replay took ~232 s versus 218 s for Round437, so no overall speedup versus the fastest matched baseline is established. The required full audit scan is not included in these replay timings.

opportunities.title: 6 · Trim trajectory persistence
opportunities.detail: Writes used 7–12 ms/match and Round424 stored about 1.8 GB for 10,000 games. Benchmark buffered compact records or chunk compression after the higher-cost action and inference paths.

opportunities.title: 7 · Keep CPU inference eager; profile feature/scorer cost
opportunities.detail: Round452 completed the full-match check of torch.compile: 13.15 games/s eager vs 4.30 compiled at eight workers, with policy inference 65.8 vs 944.6 ms/match and peak RSS 6.60 vs 11.67 GiB. Reject compiled inference in rollout workers. The single-state 1.47× gain did not transfer. Focus on feature preparation and public-counterplay scoring; see raw Round452 comparison.

opportunities.title: 8 · Reduce PPO input-construction overhead
opportunities.detail: Round453 replaced four per-slot tensor scalar reads for active volatile features with batched NumPy indexing. Full model-input construction improved 7.07% (114.73 to 106.61 ms per 1,026 states) with exact tensor parity. Linear extrapolation estimates 1.28 s saved across 162,366 states, only 0.76% of the 169.12 s Round447 sample-preparation stage; validate with a matched full PPO replay. Continue profiling transition extraction and feature assembly before scaling training.

speed.jax_decision: Round430 confirms the Showdown engine used about 18% of policy-pool match time and 8% against Public Counterplay; a simulator-only port would leave the larger measured policy, observation, and baseline-scoring costs intact. Keep Showdown as the correctness reference and require an end-to-end measured gain before a JAX/GPU engine prototype.
speed.remaining_summary: For the historical-policy pool, Showdown used about 34 ms of 193.5 ms per match (~17.5%); the remaining ~82.5% is about 159.6 ms: 84.8 ms action selection (53% of the remainder, including 73.1 ms inference), 27.4 ms observation encoding (17%), 12.6 ms trajectory writes (8%), about 10.5 ms setup (7%), 2 ms preview/first step (1%), and about 22.3 ms other overhead (14%). For Public Counterplay, the engine used about 28 ms of 359.5 ms (~8%); its scorer alone used 239 ms (67%).

remaining_components.note: Includes 73.1 ms policy inference; do not add inference again.
Repeated feature construction and static lookups.
Remaining measured episode time after named stages.

speed.worker_scaling_context: Round430 CPU rollout scaling on the 16-logical-CPU host, with 240 complete matches per setting against Max Damage. Eight workers were fastest in this short single-opponent sample; 12 and 16 workers consumed more memory and ran slower. Test batching across the existing workers before increasing worker count.

policy_inference_benchmark.context: Round430 checkpoint on 256 perspective-safe rollout states; 1 CPU thread, 5 warmups, 30 timed repeats. Timings include host-to-device transfer and action/value synchronization; collation is reported separately. Queue wait is excluded.
policy_inference_benchmark.interpretation: CUDA is slower for single states and roughly tied with CPU at batch 8, about 51% faster at batch 16, and 2.6x faster at batch 32. Queue wait is excluded. A scalar-clamp optimization reduced warm native action-feature time 41.3% (0.1983 to 0.1165 ms/state) with exact outputs against the prior NumPy-clamp implementation on 256 inputs; whole-match speed impact is not yet measured.
policy_inference_benchmark.feature_replay_caveat: The initial Round430 parity audit used initial-team opponent ordering and PPO's conditionally narrowed action mask, unlike live feature generation. New rollout data now saves per-step opponent preview order, the raw feature mask, the PPO conditional mask, and encoder version. On a fresh 64-game rollout (128 perspective records, 481 feature states), recomputation matched every saved feature value exactly. Legacy Round430 records remain missing the raw action mask, but PPO continues to train from the saved feature arrays.

counterplay_cache_benchmark.context: Same Round430 checkpoint, VGC format, 32 episode seeds, one CPU worker, and /dev/null trajectory output before and after memoizing repeated deterministic damage estimates within each joint-action score. This is a microbenchmark, not the standard 8-worker mixed-training run.
counterplay_cache_benchmark.result: Both runs produced 13 Headless P1 wins and 19 Headless P2 wins, with 0 timeouts and 0 action corrections. Policy inference averaged 31.9 vs 31.4 ms/match, observation encoding 19.5 vs 19.1 ms, and engine roundtrips 29.2 vs 28.1 ms.
counterplay_cache_benchmark.limitation: The 32-game before/after is paired on identical seeds. The 8-worker rollout validates concurrent operation but has no pre-cache 8-worker control; full 20,000-game mixed PPO throughput has not yet been remeasured.

ppo_input_preparation_benchmark.context: Round435 PPO input-preparation microbenchmark using 1,971 real transitions from 256 records. Six passes per mode; first pass excluded. CPU-only PyTorch 2.15, Python 3.12. Rollout parsing and PPO optimization excluded.
ppo_input_preparation_benchmark.estimate_context: Linear extrapolation from microbenchmark saving to 162,366 transitions, compared with 151.5 s PPO sample collection; not an end-to-end training measurement.

rollout_extraction_microbenchmark.context: Round435 Max Damage shard: 256 records and 1,971 trainable transitions, seven passes per implementation with the first excluded. CPU-only PyTorch 2.15 / Python 3.12; transition extraction only.
rollout_extraction_microbenchmark.estimate_context: Linear extrapolation from a single Max Damage shard sample to 162,366 transitions; not a full PPO timing.

ppo_full_update_replay.context: Round441 replayed the exact Round435 20k rollout data on the RTX 4060 with 1,272 PPO steps. Model metrics and all 82 checkpoint tensors were bit-identical to Round437.
ppo_full_update_replay.finding: Round441 was slower than both prior replays. Runtime conditions differ, so this is not evidence that the code changes caused the regression; the isolated microbenchmark gains are not yet confirmed end to end. PPO record parsing/preparation remains the largest measured stage.

ppo_observation_array_reuse_benchmark.context: Round435 Max Damage shard: 256 records and 1,971 transitions, seven passes with first excluded. CUDA Torch 2.15 / Python 3.12; transition extraction only.
ppo_observation_array_reuse_benchmark.estimate_context: Linear extrapolation to 162,366 transitions. Added after the Round441 full replay; this change is not yet included in end-to-end training timing.

ppo_hidden_target_precompute_benchmark.context: Round435 Max Damage shard: 256 records and 1,971 transitions, seven passes with first excluded. CUDA Torch 2.15 / Python 3.12; transition extraction only.
ppo_hidden_target_precompute_benchmark.estimate_context: Linear extrapolation to 162,366 transitions. Added after Round441 and not included in an end-to-end PPO replay.

ppo_offset_index_replay.context: Round447 used byte offsets emitted by a fresh strict audit to seek directly to the 20,000 valid trainable views in the 3.87 GiB Round435 rollout set. Each selected row was still fully checked against the closed-sheet perspective and trajectory contract.
ppo_offset_index_replay.finding: Sample preparation was 57.15 s faster than Round441, but Round447 full replay was about 14 s slower than Round437. This is a promising reduction against Round441, not a confirmed end-to-end speedup against the fastest matched baseline; the strict audit pass is also excluded from the replay total.
ppo_offset_index_replay.integrity_note: Round444 was excluded: skipping validation admitted one incomplete row, producing 20,001 records and 162,374 transitions. Round447 used audited offsets and full row validation; future training now checks actual prepared transitions against the audited count before checkpoint save.

live_team_cache_benchmark.context: Round448 compared the live input encoder with and without the per-agent static team-token cache on 1,971 real Round435 transitions from 256 match records. The cached path is now wired into both ordinary and paired PolicyAgent inference.
live_team_cache_benchmark.scope_note: Model-input construction only; no full-match games/sec or p95 decision-latency comparison yet.

shared_inference_queue_benchmark.context: Round449 queue-aware prototype using 256 real closed-sheet inputs from Round435, 64 requests per concurrent producer, and the Round447 checkpoint. CPU baseline used independent processes (one Torch thread each); GPU used one shared CUDA queue. Inputs were prebuilt, so these are upper bounds for production throughput.
shared_inference_queue_benchmark.finding: At both 8 and 16 producers, the shared GPU queue was slower and had higher p95 latency than independent CPU processes. Waiting 3 ms for batches reduced GPU throughput further. Do not implement a shared GPU broker at the current worker counts; its actual performance would also include IPC and live feature preparation.
shared_inference_queue_benchmark.scope_note: Inputs were already in memory. The shared queue includes batch collation, H2D transfer, model forward, output synchronization and queue latency, but excludes IPC serialization and rollout think time; results are an upper bound for production service throughput.

cpu_inference_followups.context: Round450 and Round451 used the Round447 checkpoint and 256 real closed-sheet Round435 states; measurements cover full native action selection but are microbenchmarks, not complete matches.

compiled_policy.status: Rejected for rollout use: the full-match run was slower despite exact action parity in the earlier microbenchmark.

dynamic_int8.status: Rejected for now: slower and 1.95% action disagreement.

cpu_inference_followups.next_step: Keep eager CPU inference. The matched eight-worker Round452 full-match run measured 13.15 games/s eager vs 4.30 compiled; policy inference was 65.8 vs 944.6 ms/match, and peak RSS was 6.60 vs 11.67 GiB. Focus next on observation/action feature preparation and public-counterplay scoring; only revisit compilation after explaining repeated compile/runtime overhead.

full_match_compile_benchmark.context: Round452 compared eager and torch.compile CPU inference on the Round430 checkpoint with the same seed, episode offsets, eight workers, and Max Damage opponent; 64 complete matches per condition. Includes process startup and compilation.
full_match_compile_benchmark.finding: The single-state torch.compile advantage did not transfer to rollout workers. Cold eight-worker complete-match throughput fell from 13.15 to 4.30 games/s; measured policy inference rose from about 65.8 to 944.6 ms/match and peak RSS rose from 6.60 to 11.67 GiB. Keep compilation disabled for training. This small run is a speed comparison, not a strength evaluation.
full_match_compile_benchmark.limitations: Each condition ran 64 matches and included process startup and compilation. Same seeds and episode offsets were used; policy action sampling and game randomness mean match outcomes are not a powered strength comparison. Test set was a short Max Damage workload, not the full opponent mixture.

ppo_preparation_optimization.context: Round447 prepared 162,366 transitions from 20,000 games in 169.12 s; full replay was about 232 s and matched Round437 checkpoint tensors exactly. Round453 optimized one measured input-encoding substage; current 16.49 games/s complete training-iteration baseline remains Round430.
ppo_preparation_optimization.scope_note: 1,026 real states, seven repeats after warm-up. Linear extrapolation only; no full PPO replay has measured the net change yet.
ppo_preparation_optimization.matched_replay_context: The complete PPO replay preserved all metrics and model tensors. Sample collection was 6.05 s (3.58%) faster than Round447; the whole replay was about 3.36 s faster than Round447 but remains slower than Round437’s 217.98 s. One matched replay cannot separate the code change from run-to-run variance or attribute all observed savings to the NumPy encoder; repeat the matched comparison before claiming reliable end-to-end throughput gain.

latest_run.status: matched PPO replay · exact model parity
latest_run.summary: Round453 replayed the audited 20,000-game Round435 set with 162,366 transitions. Sample preparation took 163.07 s vs Round447’s 169.12 s; all metrics and all 82 checkpoint tensors matched exactly. Full update wall time was 228.64 s vs about 232 s in Round447, but remains slower than Round437’s 217.98 s. One replay does not establish a reliable end-to-end speedup. Round430 remains the validated in-battle candidate.
latest_run.evaluation: Exact replay parity; no strength change

method: Native self-play PPO for in-battle decisions. Terminal win/loss remains the main objective; win-probability and hidden-set prediction are auxiliary tasks. Search comes after a stronger policy.
jax_decision: Round430 has a confirmed self-play head-to-head lift over Round424, but external-opponent screens remain inconclusive. Prioritize measured inference batching, observation throughput, and rollouts; keep equilibrium-oriented opponent coverage and defer a JAX/GPU engine rewrite until its end-to-end payoff is measured.
evaluation_note: Score rates include wins and half credit for draws. Use paired held-out teams, side swaps, repeated outcomes, and cluster intervals. Track results across public counterplay, random, historical PPO, and Max Damage; no one matchup percentage is the finish line. Round431's equal-weight four-opponent mean was 59.86%, but the median was 48.05%, p10 47.30%, and worst score 47.07%; the mean is lifted by random play. All paired differences vs Round430 included zero.
